Adding COinS Metadata for Zotero

Peter Baumgartner

2026-08-23

Source: vignettes/add-coins.Rmd
add-coins.Rmd

What is COinS?

COinS stands for ContextObjects in Spans. It’s a simple, standardized way to embed bibliographic metadata directly into HTML pages so that specialized software can read and extract it.

Think of it like this: when you visit a website, humans see the text and can understand what a blog post is about. But reference managers like Zotero need machine-readable metadata to know the title, author, publication date, and other citation details without requiring manual data entry.

COinS solves this by embedding bibliographic information in an invisible HTML <span> element on your page. When Zotero visits your blog post, it detects the COinS metadata and can automatically add the post to your library with all the correct fields filled in.

Why Use COinS?

The Problem

Without COinS, Zotero has to guess your post’s metadata by examining the HTML structure. This often fails for blog posts because:

  • Blog post titles might be in an <h1> tag, but so might many other things
  • The publication date might be hidden in an obscure <time> element or embedded in a longer text string
  • Authors are rarely marked up consistently across different blog platforms
  • Categories or tags have no standard HTML representation

The Solution

COinS eliminates guessing. When you add a COinS span to your post, Zotero can:

  1. Automatically detect the post’s metadata — no manual entry needed
  2. Save the post to your personal library — with correct author, date, title, and keywords
  3. Use correct citation formatting — because Zotero knows the post is a blog article, not a book or journal article
  4. Reference it in your writing — Zotero generates correct citations in your preferred style (Chicago, APA, etc.)

This is especially valuable for academic writers who rely on reference managers for literature management.

The Metadata in COinS

A COinS entry is built from key-value pairs that describe a published work. The main fields for a blog post are:

Field Example Purpose
rft.title “My Amazing Discovery” Article title
rft.au “Peter Baumgartner” Author name
rft.date “2026-08-22” Publication date
rft.genre “blogPost” Content type (in this case, a blog post)
rft_val_fmt “info:ofi/fmt:kev:mtx:journal” Standard identifier for the metadata format
rft.description “A brief summary…” Post description or abstract
rft.keywords “research, data science” Categories or tags
ctx_ver “Z39.88-2004” COinS specification version

Additional optional fields can include: - rft.pub — Publication/blog name - rft.spage, rft.epage — Page numbers (not applicable to blog posts) - rft.issn — Journal ISSN (not applicable to blog posts) - rft.language — Language code (e.g., “en-US”)

The Standard Behind COinS

COinS is based on the OpenURL standard (ANSI/NISO Z39.88-2004), which was originally designed to help libraries link users to full-text content. The “ContextObject” is the standardized metadata package at the heart of OpenURL.

The clever part of COinS is that it embeds an OpenURL ContextObject invisibly in HTML using a <span> element:

<span class="Z3988" title="ctx_ver=Z39.88-2004&rft.title=...&rft.au=..."></span>

The class="Z3988" tells processors like Zotero that this span contains COinS metadata. The actual data is in the title attribute (which is counterintuitive—it’s not displayed as a tooltip; it’s just a container for the encoded metadata).

Why a span?

Using a <span> allows COinS metadata to be placed anywhere in a web page without breaking the HTML structure or being visible to human readers. Other approaches (like storing metadata in <meta> tags in the page’s <head>) are more restrictive—you can only have one set of metadata per page. With COinS, you can embed metadata for multiple items on the same page.

Websites Using COinS

COinS has been adopted by many major platforms and content providers:

  • Wikipedia — embedded in citation templates and bibliographic data
  • Academic repositories — CiteULike, Citebase, Hubmed, ResearchGate
  • Library catalogs — Copac, WorldCat, VuFind
  • Publishing platforms — WordPress blogs, Institutional repositories
  • Specialized services — Zotero itself can generate COinS for shared bibliographies

How Zotero Uses COinS

When you’re browsing a blog post with COinS in your Zotero-enabled browser:

  1. Zotero’s browser extension scans the page and finds the <span class="Z3988"> element
  2. It decodes the embedded metadata
  3. It displays a save icon (📖) in your browser address bar, indicating that Zotero can capture the page
  4. You click the icon to save the post to your library
  5. Zotero populates the entry with all the metadata from COinS: title, author, date, description, etc.

Without COinS, Zotero might not recognize the page as a citable item, and you’d have to manually enter all the metadata.

Adding COinS to Your Blog Posts

The add_coins() function automates COinS generation. Here’s how to use it:

Prerequisites

  • A completed Quarto blog post in posts/your-post/index.qmd
  • A _quarto.yml file in your blog’s root directory with at least site-url: specified
  • Optional: configuration in your project’s .Rprofile

Basic Usage 

library(qpost)

# Add COinS metadata to the currently open post in RStudio
add_coins()

# Or specify a file path explicitly
add_coins(file_path = "posts/my-post/index.qmd")

With configuration

Set up your blog’s metadata in the project .Rprofile:

# Project-level .Rprofile
options(
  qpost.lang = "en",          # Language code (auto-detected from _quarto.yml if present)
  qpost.license = "CC-BY-4.0" # Creative Commons license for your blog posts
)

Then call add_coins() as above.

What add_coins() Does

When you call add_coins(file_path):

  1. Reads your post’s YAML front matter — extracts title, author, date, categories, description, etc.
  2. Queries _quarto.yml — reads the blog’s site URL and language settings
  3. Applies auto-resolution — fills in missing fields from defaults:
    • language — from post YAML → from _quarto.yml → from getOption("qpost.lang") → omitted
    • license — from post YAML → from getOption("qpost.license") → omitted
  4. Generates the COinS metadata — creates the properly formatted key-value string
  5. Creates an R code chunk — appends a chunk to your post that displays the metadata
  6. Opens the edited post — so you can review and commit the changes

Generated Output

At the bottom of your index.qmd, add_coins() appends:

This code: - Uses an R chunk with echo: false and results: asis so it’s invisible to readers - Outputs the COinS <span> as raw HTML - Is placed at the end of your post, so Zotero sees the complete content first

The Metadata in Detail

Here’s what each key means in the generated COinS:

ctx_ver=Z39.88-2004

Specifies the COinS/OpenURL version.

rft_val_fmt=info:ofi/fmt:kev:mtx:journal

Declares the metadata format as “key-encoded-value” (kev) for a journal-like resource. We use this for blog posts because they’re closest to journal articles in structure.

rft.genre=blogPost

Identifies the resource type as a blog post (not a book, journal article, or conference paper).

rft.atitle=My%20Amazing%20Discovery

The article title (URL-encoded, so spaces become %20).

rft.au=Peter%20Baumgartner

The author name.

rft.date=2026-08-22

Publication date in ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD).

rft.description=A%20brief%20summary...

Post description or abstract (optional).

rft.language=en

Language code (optional). Defaults to your blog’s language from _quarto.yml.

rft.keywords=research%2Cdata%20science

Categories/tags from your post (comma-separated, URL-encoded).

rft.license=CC-BY-4.0

License identifier (optional). Set in .Rprofile to apply the same license to all posts.

Configuration

Auto-resolution Hierarchy

add_coins() builds metadata using this priority order:

Field Source priority
title Post YAML title: (required)
date Post YAML date: (required)
author Post YAML author:
description Post YAML description:
categories/keywords Post YAML categories:
language (1) Post YAML lang: → (2) _quarto.yml lang: → (3) getOption("qpost.lang") → omitted
license (1) Post YAML license: → (2) getOption("qpost.license") → omitted
site/blog name _quarto.yml title:
site URL _quarto.yml site-url:

This means: - If your _quarto.yml already specifies a language, you don’t need to configure qpost.lang - You only need to set qpost.license once in your .Rprofile to apply it to all posts - Post-level YAML always overrides defaults

Example .Rprofile 

# Project-level .Rprofile (in your blog's root directory)

# These settings apply to add_coins() for this project
options(
  qpost.lang = "en",           # Fallback language for posts without lang: in YAML
  qpost.license = "CC-BY-4.0"  # License for blog post content
)

Editing COinS After Creation

The COinS span is just an R code chunk at the end of your post. You can:

  1. Edit it manually — change metadata values directly in the title attribute
  2. Regenerate it — delete the chunk and run add_coins() again
  3. Remove it — delete the chunk entirely (though this defeats the purpose!)

To re-run add_coins() on an existing post: 1. Delete the coins code chunk at the bottom 2. Run add_coins(file_path = "posts/your-post/index.qmd") 3. Review and commit the changes

Backup Mode

By default, add_coins(backup = TRUE) creates a backup of your post before modifying it:

add_coins(file_path = "posts/my-post/index.qmd", backup = TRUE)

This creates a file like posts/my-post/index.qmd.bak as a safety measure. If something goes wrong, you can restore the original.

To disable backups:

add_coins(file_path = "posts/my-post/index.qmd", backup = FALSE)

Testing Your COinS

Once you’ve added COinS to a post, you can test it:

  1. Render your blog with quarto preview or quarto render
  2. Open the post in your browser
  3. Install Zotero browser extension (if you haven’t already) from zotero.org
  4. Click the Zotero save icon in your browser address bar
  5. Verify the metadata — Zotero should pre-fill the title, author, date, and other fields automatically

If the save icon doesn’t appear, check that: - The HTML output contains the COinS <span> (view page source in your browser) - The metadata in the title attribute is properly URL-encoded - Your Zotero browser extension is enabled

Integration with Academic Workflow

COinS is particularly valuable if you:

  • Write papers that cite your own blog posts — Zotero can cite them with proper formatting
  • Build a personal knowledge base — Zotero can organize your posts alongside other research
  • Share research — Others can easily add your posts to their Zotero libraries
  • Track citations — Zotero note-taking features work with your posts as regular bibliographic items
